newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: High NZ dlr burning issue for suffering exporters.
newsitem.headline: High NZ dlr burning issue for suffering exporters.

text.p: The high value of the New Zealand dollar is undermining earnings in all exporting industries, and many cannot lift productivity sufficiently to combat its effects, exporters' groups said on Thursday.
Eleven groups met in Wellington for an all-day summit on responses to the "crisis situation" facing New Zealand exporters due to the high level of the currency.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash addressed the summit, but his speech was off the record.

"The main point I want to reflect by our being here is to recognise the considerable pressure that exporters are under, but beyond that I don't want to say any more at this point," Brash told reporters.
The Dairy Board said New Zealand dollar had appreciated 27 percent against the U.S. currency in the last three years, negating much of the benefit of increased added-value sales.

"No industry can expect to increase selling prices, or cut costs to that extent on an ongoing basis." The board said while short-term fluctuations could be offset by hedging, the Kiwi's rapid rise could not be guarded against for long periods.

The Fruitgrowers Federation said the Kiwi had also appreciated sharply against the other currencies in which the fruit industry trades -- mark, sterling and yen. A careful foreign exchange hedging programme had been able to cushion significantly the Kiwi's impact on the industry.
"However we do not regard ourselves as foreign exchange operators and it is just simply not possible to continue to absorb such increases," the federation said.
Wools of New Zealand said the average overseas processor of NZ wool was paying 30 percent more than they were just over four years ago, but New Zealand woolgrowers received the same price.
"Productivity and competitiveness gains cannot hope to outrun an exchange rate which is appreciating at the rate of seven percent per annum," it said.
The Dairy Board and Federated Farmers both said while they supported the government's policy of seeking price stability, they were concerned at the method by which it was achieved.
The Dairy Board blamed the rise in the exchange rate largely on the tight monetary policy exercised in the government's attempt to control inflation.
"Monetary policy is the only instrument used in controlling inflation at present and is a blunt instrument. A broader range of economic objectives needs to be employed to control inflation," it said.
Federated Farmers said while it remained a "staunch supporter" of the Reserve Bank Act, that was not an endorsement of the way the RBNZ had conducted its monetary policy.

"Federated Farmers firmly believes that monetary policy is being asked to do too much. The only tools the Reserve Bank has are interest rates and exchange rates which impact harshly upon the export sectors."

It argued the government must implement policies to defeat inflation at source, by addressing inflation-generating issues such as a lack of household savings, local and central government rates and charges, and accident compensation levies.

The Manufacturers Federation said an overvalued exchange rate affected manufacturers on the domestic market as well as in their export markets, because the price of competing imports was depressed by an overvalued currency.
